At her hips hung two long white cases, each as long as her leg. When she flew, they opened into wings. She had built the rest herself, with an old engineer. It was a small, strong motor, a coil of fine steel cable and a grapple that fired like a bullet. Two swords lay on her back. Every flight was written in her black drill-book.
She fired at the signal mast and flew up the cable like a dolphin.

Once, in a street of rubble, he had lifted her onto his shoulders. "Don't look down, Fan," he said. "Look at me."
All she wanted was to stand beside him and fight. So she trained until her hands bled. Still, a knot of doubt sat in her.
I could never quite reach his level.
But she carried one hope like a lantern in the wind.
If I never stop, maybe one day I will.

Lesley's face softened. She turned away. "That man talks too much. Come to my office tomorrow at six. And don't let go of whatever you were holding."

On Friday, the weekly ranking went up outside the training hall. Layla came early, sure she was first.
She read it three times. She had seen Fanny in the drills, running along the wall and even the ceiling. She had told herself it was luck.

There were contests of every kind. In a cleaning-duty race, both girls crawled along a corridor with mops. In a race down the tower stair, Fanny, who had never lost a descent, was beaten by a banister.
After one contest they lay on the grass. "I think I'm getting better," said Fanny. "Because of you. Now I'm finding out how much more there is."
Fanny never minded losing, so Layla could not even hate her. And a cold suspicion crept in. Maybe all the contests were a way of being near her. She put the thought away in a drawer.
